idiom_name: pointer-to-data-member lens template (V C::*) with copy-and-set
implementation_notes: C++ ships no optics, so the classic realization is hand-written: a template stores an inner projection as a pointer to data member (`V C::*`), reads it with `object.*member` and returns an updated copy whose focus was replaced, and a composition template nests the two projections (C++17's `std::invoke` can apply a pointer-to-member as a callable, which makes the setter generic). What most code actually needs is the two-statement copy - `auto copy = p; copy.home.city = "Berlin";` - and that is the right choice for a single fixed path; the template earns its place only when one focus is stored, passed or composed across many call sites, and it is not worth pulling in a dependency for that.
pitfalls: A lens holding `V C::*` keeps no owner alive: a lens whose whole outlives the object it was built from reads freed members - the pointer is a projection, not a reference.
Copy-and-set is shallow at container boundaries: `std::vector` members are deep-copied, `std::shared_ptr`/raw pointer members are not, so an "immutable" update can still alias state.
Pointers to members of virtual bases, or through an ambiguous base, are ill-formed or need an explicit cast; the template silently stops composing there.

variants.name: Boost.PFR index-based reflection lens (C++14)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.PFR (available since Boost 1.75) exposes aggregate members by index without macros or member pointers - `boost::pfr::tuple_size<T>`, `boost::pfr::get<I>(value)` - so one generic lens template can address any aggregate field positionally and be generated in a loop over indices, which is what serialisation, diffing and schema-driven code need. The costs are structural: only aggregates qualify (no private members, no user-declared constructors), the focus is positional rather than named so it does not survive field reordering, and the reflection layer worsens compile times and diagnostics. Prefer the member-pointer variant when the fields can be named, and this one only when the set of fields is genuinely dynamic.
pitfalls: Positional foci break silently when fields are reordered or inserted - the code still compiles and updates the wrong member.
Non-aggregates (private members, user-declared constructors, base classes) simply do not reflect; the failure shows up as a template error deep inside Boost.PFR.
The reflection layer multiplies template instantiations, so compile time and error-message size grow with every field position that is used.
